checks.claim: Key: rubbing a rubber balloon on hair moves electrons from the hair onto the balloon
checks.note: Science Learning Hub: 'electrons are moved from the hair to the surface of the balloon'. Hair sits well above rubber balloon in classroom triboelectric series (Carolina, Physics Classroom).

checks.claim: The balloon ends negative and the hair positive (short of electrons)
checks.note: 'The balloon becomes negatively charged'; hair 'positively charged (fewer electrons than before)'.

checks.claim: Hair gives up electrons more easily than rubber (triboelectric order)
checks.note: Hair near the positive end, rubber balloon toward the negative end in school series; series are approximate, but the hair/balloon pair is consistent across sources.

checks.claim: Wrong: electrons moved from the balloon onto the hair
checks.note: Opposite of the standard result; not defensible at this level.

checks.claim: Wrong (both): protons moved between balloon and hair; protons stay in the nucleus
checks.note: OpenStax: positive charge 'is carried by the proton, which is stuck firmly in the nucleus of atoms'; rubbing increases the transfer of electrons.

checks.claim: Context: rubbing makes no new charge, only moves electrons
checks.note: 'The law of conservation of charge says that electrical charge cannot be created or destroyed.'

checks.claim: Key: two balloons rubbed on the same hair carry like charge and repel
checks.note: 'Like charges repel, whereas unlike charges attract.' Both balloons gain electrons from the same hair, so both are negative.

checks.claim: Wrong: unlike charges push each other away
checks.note: Unlike charges attract.

checks.claim: Wrong (both): magnetic poles push the balloons apart
checks.note: A rubbed balloon is electrically charged, not magnetised; the force is electrostatic.

checks.claim: Context: more charge, harder push; the force weakens with distance; unlike magnetic poles attract
checks.note: Coulomb force proportional to the product of the charges and falls with distance; OpenStax 22-1: 'like poles repel and unlike poles attract'.

checks.claim: Key: the balloon's charge polarises the neutral wall, drawing opposite charge nearer
checks.note: OpenStax: in an insulator 'the distribution of charge in atoms and molecules is shifted slightly'; 'Opposite charge is attracted nearer ... while like charge is repelled'; polarization is 'the separation of charges in an object that remains neutral'.

checks.claim: Context: nearer opposite charge pulls harder than the farther like charge pushes, since force weakens with distance
checks.note: Stated by OpenStax as the reason the neutral object is attracted overall.

checks.claim: Wrong: its charge flows into the wall and holds it
checks.note: The wall is an insulator so the charge stays on the balloon; if charge flowed away, the attraction would be lost, not gained.

checks.claim: Wrong: air pressure pins it; the rubbing made it a weak magnet
checks.note: The hold is electrostatic induction (polarisation), not air pressure or magnetism.

checks.claim: Context: pressed to a metal door, the balloon loses its charge into the metal and falls
checks.note: Scientific American / Science Buddies: on metal 'the extra electrons in the balloon quickly leave the balloon and move into the metal', so it does not adhere. A fair 8th-grade statement.

checks.claim: Key: the small magnet wins because it is close and its field fades fast with distance
checks.note: Dipole field 'falls off inversely with the cube of the distance from the magnet's center'.

checks.claim: Context: Earth's surface field is weak
checks.note: 'about 25 to 65 microtesla'.

checks.claim: Context: a few cm from a small bar magnet its field is many times Earth's; across the room it is far below
checks.note: Good bar magnet m = 0.1 A m^2 (Wikipedia). On-axis B = 2e-8/r^3 T gives about 0.74 mT at 3 cm (about 15x Earth's ~50 uT) and about 0.02 uT at 1 m. Holds for a typical classroom bar magnet.

checks.claim: Wrong: it is a stronger magnet than the whole of Earth
checks.note: Earth's dipole moment ~8 x 10^22 A m^2 vs ~0.1 A m^2 for a good bar magnet.

checks.claim: Wrong: its magnetism is a different kind from Earth's
checks.note: Earth's field resembles 'a giant bar magnet'; both are magnetic fields acting on the same needle.

checks.claim: Wrong: it shields the needle; context: the fields add and the needle follows the sum
checks.note: 'the total field at any point is the vector sum of the fields produced by individual sources'; compass shows field by 'alignment with the local magnetic vector'.

checks.claim: William Gilbert was an English physician
checks.note: 'an English physician, physicist, and natural philosopher'.

checks.claim: Terrella: a lodestone shaped into a ball, a 'little Earth'
checks.note: Made from 'a naturally occurring lodestone' shaped into a ball; Gilbert called it a 'little Earth'.

checks.claim: A pivoted needle over it lined up with the ball's poles and dipped toward the surface, more steeply nearer the poles, as on Earth
checks.note: 'iron needles align precisely along meridians converging at the poles'; dip increases toward the poles, vertical at the poles. Wikipedia De Magnete: level at the equator, dip 'increases towards the poles'. Dip on Earth was found by Robert Norman, 1581 (Grokipedia Terrella).

checks.claim: De Magnete published 1600
checks.note: Published 1600 in London by Peter Short.

checks.claim: Key: Gilbert concluded Earth itself is a giant magnet
checks.note: He concluded 'Earth was itself magnetic', 'the reason why compasses point north'; Grokipedia: 'the Earth functions as a giant magnet'.

checks.claim: Wrong: Pole Star draws needles; magnetic island at the North Pole (older explanations he set aside)
checks.note: Before him some held compasses pointed to 'the pole-star Polaris, or a large magnetic island on the north pole'; Grokipedia De Magnete: he rejected attributing magnetism to stars and the magnetic-mountain/island tales.

checks.claim: Wrong: a needle seeks the north by its own nature
checks.note: Not his conclusion: De Magnete gave 'the first rational explanation' of north-pointing: 'the Earth itself was magnetic'.

checks.claim: The North Magnetic Pole is in the Arctic, where the field points straight down
checks.note: Field 'directed vertically downward'; WMM 2025 position 85.762 N, 139.298 E, Arctic Ocean.

checks.claim: Key: it is a magnetic south pole, since unlike poles attract
checks.note: 'the magnetic pole that is near the geographic North Pole is actually a south magnetic pole'; 'like poles repel and unlike poles attract'. Grokipedia: it 'functions as a magnetic south pole'.

checks.claim: Wrong: north pole since like poles attract; north pole since it lies in the north
checks.note: Like poles repel; the name comes from the compass end that points there, not its kind.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Neither, since plain iron draws either end'; context: plain iron would draw either end
checks.note: NASA (Stern): ordinary iron is 'always attracted to a magnet', becoming 'a temporary magnet, of a polarity suitable for attraction'. A compass's S end turning south rules plain iron out.

checks.claim: Oersted, April 1820, University of Copenhagen, during a lecture
checks.note: Grokipedia: 21 April 1820, lecture demonstration at the University of Copenhagen; Linda Hall: 21 April 'according to tradition'. Oersted's own later account (quoted at skullsinthestars.com/2011/04/03/the-birth-of-electromagnetism-1820/) says the first trial was made 'in the presence of the audience'. Wikipedia calls the story that he found it 'incidentally' during a lecture a myth; the stem does not say 'by accident', so it is safe.

checks.claim: The wire was held just above the compass needle; the needle was under glass
checks.note: Oersted's account: 'a very thin platina wire, which was placed over a compass covered with glass'. Grokipedia: wire 'positioned above a compass needle covered by glass'.

checks.claim: Closing the circuit swung the needle from north; open circuit, no deflection
checks.note: 'No deflection occurred when the circuit was open or the current absent'; Wikipedia: needle 'deflected from magnetic north by a nearby electric current'.

checks.claim: Key: the current in the wire made a magnetic field
checks.note: 'an electric current produces a circular magnetic field as it flows through a wire'.

checks.claim: Wrong: the needle's field made a current; the plates were magnets; current leaked into the needle
checks.note: The battery made the current; copper and zinc are not ferromagnetic; the glass-covered needle was outside the circuit and the effect passes through glass and wood (Oersted 1820, quoted at skullsinthestars).

checks.claim: Context: battery of copper and zinc plates
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a pile of approximately 20 copper and zinc plates'. Oersted's own account calls the lecture battery a small 'galvanic trough', which in that era was copper and zinc; fine.

checks.claim: Context: first proof that electricity and magnetism are linked
checks.note: MagLab: 'the first indication most scientists had regarding the electricity-magnetism connection'; Linda Hall: before this 'no one found any magnetic effects of electrical current'. Romagnosi's 1802 report is usually read as electrostatic and unpublished, so the mainstream claim stands.

checks.claim: Context: later tests that year showed the field runs in circles around the wire
checks.note: Linda Hall: 'an electric current generates a circular magnetic field around a wire'; Oersted's July 1820 paper: 'this conflict performs circles'.

checks.claim: Key: more turns of the same wire (same current) makes the electromagnet stronger
checks.note: Strength 'quantified as ampere-turns (product of current and turns)'. Winding the loose part of the same wire keeps the circuit's resistance and so the current the same, as the context says. NGSS MS-PS2-3 names this test.

checks.claim: Wrong: reversing the battery only swaps the poles
checks.note: 'To change the poles, just change which way the battery is hooked up. This changes the direction the current flows and reverses the field.' Same current, same strength.

checks.claim: Wrong: copper nail; pulling the nail out
checks.note: 'A core can increase the magnetic field to thousands of times the strength of the field of the coil alone'; copper is not ferromagnetic (Grokipedia, Ferromagnetism).

checks.claim: Context: Joseph Henry wound silk-covered wire in many layers to get more turns
checks.note: Henry used 'wire insulated by silk thread', letting him wind multiple layers; Sturgeon's bare wire allowed only one spaced layer, limiting turns.

checks.claim: Maglock: electromagnet in the frame grips a steel plate on the door; about 1,200 lb; no moving parts
checks.note: Electromagnet on the frame and armature plate on the door; holding force 600 to over 2,000 lb, standard 1,200 to 1,500 lbf; 'no moving parts to wear out'.

checks.claim: Key: when power fails the grip vanishes at once and the door comes free
checks.note: 'the lock releases instantly when power is interrupted'. Grokipedia also notes slight residual magnetism can delay release; 'at once' is a fair 8th-grade simplification.

checks.claim: Wrong: holds on; fades over hours; turns to a push
checks.note: 'The magnetic field disappears when the current is turned off'; an unpowered coil neither holds nor repels.

checks.claim: Context: fail-safe, nobody trapped in a fire alarm or power cut
checks.note: 'inherently fail-safe', 'free egress in emergencies such as fire alarms or power outages'.

checks.claim: Context: a scrapyard crane drops its steel when the current to its electromagnet is switched off
checks.note: Crane magnets 'lift ferrous loads weighing several tons', 'de-energized to release the material at the destination'.

unit_notes: All nine questions check out. Optional wording only, not an error: in d8fefb6a7e, real maglock power supplies often carry a standby battery, so a sharp reader could say the lock holds through a building blackout; 'if the power to the lock fails' would close that gap. In 76305809c8, the stem rightly avoids the 'found it by accident' myth (Wikipedia calls it a myth); keep it that way. Q1's electrons-from-hair-to-balloon follows the school model and every main source; one University of Wisconsin demo page that calls the balloon positive is an outlier.
